content.title: Acute Coronary Syndromes (selected excerpt)
content.summary: Guidance on initial pre-hospital assessment and time-critical management of patients with suspected acute coronary syndromes (ACS), with emphasis on ECG-based triage into STEMI vs non-STEMI pathways, prompt reperfusion for STEMI, and the importance of minimizing time to treatment.
content.initial_assessment: If the first responding medical professional suspects ACS, acquire and analyse a 12-lead ECG as soon as possible. EMS personnel should have access to defibrillation and be trained in basic cardiac life support.
content.ECG_triage: Patients with suspected ACS are initially categorized using the 12-lead ECG into two treatment pathways: (i) ECG consistent with STEMI (persistent ST-segment elevation or equivalent ECG patterns) and (ii) patients without ST-segment elevation or equivalent patterns (suspected NSTE-ACS). Initial ECG-guided risk stratification should inform treatment decisions, target hospital selection, and timing of invasive coronary angiography (ICA).
content.immediate_management: Suspected STEMI indicates higher risk of immediate life-threatening complications (e.g., ventricular fibrillation) and supports initiating emergency reperfusion strategy with direct transfer to a centre with 24/7 PCI capabilities.
content.time_to_treatment: Time to treatment is vital for patients triaged to the STEMI pathway. Components of total ischemic time, contributors to delays, and selection of reperfusion strategy should be continuously audited using quality indicators (QIs). If projected QIs are not met, interventions are required to improve system performance.
content.community_recognition: Recognition of ischemic symptoms by the public is crucial to activate out-of-hospital pathways. The recommended action is to contact EMS rather than self-present to ED or primary care. Community education should target underserved groups and avoid biased messaging based on sex, ethnicity, or socioeconomic status.
content.socioeconomic_and_demographic_considerat: Time from symptom onset to first call for help is associated with socioeconomic factors and sex. Public health messaging and targeted initiatives should address delays in recognition and response among deprived or minority communities.
content.references_and_figures: References to Recommendation Table 4, Figure 7, and Figure 8 are made for full details and treatment times/algorithms. A slide download/open-in-new-tab option is mentioned on the page.
